title: Market Microstructure Assessment
description: Order books, matching rules, spreads, adverse selection and execution costs. All books and fills are clearly hypothetical.

questions.prompt: A stock quotes 100.00 bid / 100.04 ask. What is the quoted spread in **basis points** of the mid? (Integer.)
questions.explanation: Spread = 0.04 on a mid of 100.02 → 0.04/100.02 ≈ 4bp. Spread-in-bps normalises across price levels, which is why it is the standard quoting unit.

questions.prompt: You cross that spread with a 5,000,000-notional market order (and the book absorbs it at the touch). What is the **half-spread cost** in dollars? (Integer, no commas.)
questions.explanation: $5{,}000{,}000 \times 0.0004 / 2 = \$1{,}000$: the instantaneous loss versus the mid, the moment the trade prints.

questions.prompt: Book: bid depth 4,500 lots, ask depth 2,400 lots (within the near levels). What is the order-book **imbalance** $(B-A)/(B+A)$? (Three decimals.)
questions.explanation: $(4500-2400)/(4500+2400) = 2100/6900 = 0.304$ — roughly 30% more resting buy interest; a classic (noisy) short-horizon signal.

questions.prompt: A 500-lot market buy arrives. Best ask is 100.02 × 900. At what price does it fill?
questions.explanation: The aggressor fills at the resting order's price — price priority takes you to the best ask, and the match price is the passive side's price. The book thins by 500 at 100.02; the spread is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Two limit orders rest at the same price. Which fills first when an arriving order takes that level?
options: the one whose owner trades more volume
questions.explanation: Price priority first, then FIFO within a price level. Queue position is why cancel-replace strategies pay a real cost: rejoining the queue loses your place.

questions.prompt: Your market buy executes at 100.04; a moment later the mid is 100.05. What is the **effective spread** $2|P_{exec} - M_{post}|$? (Give the answer in cents, two decimals — e.g. 3.25.)
questions.explanation: $2 \times |100.04 - 100.05| = 0.02$: 2 cents. The post-trade mid is the honest benchmark — measuring against the pre-trade mid hides the adverse move your own information caused.

questions.prompt: A strategy's winning months sum to +16.0% and its losing months to −6.5%. What is its **profit factor**? (Two decimals.)
questions.explanation: $16.0 / 6.5 = 2.46$: gross wins over gross losses. Above ~1.5 with a real sample is respectable; above 2.5 on months (not trades) deserves suspicion of a lucky sample.

questions.prompt: You are making a market and a well-informed client repeatedly lifts your offer. The textbook response ladder is:
options: keep quotes fixed: consistency builds trust
widen or fade quotes on one-sided flow, adjust inventory, step aside if toxicity persists
increase size at the same prices to average the flow
questions.explanation: Adverse selection management: measure flow toxicity, skew or widen when flow is one-sided, lean inventory the other way, and withdraw when the edge against you persists. Holding quotes fixed donates the spread (and worse) to informed flow.

questions.prompt: The square-root impact law predicts that doubling your order size (same ADV) increases impact by approximately:
options: no change: impact depends only on ADV
questions.explanation: Impact $\propto \sqrt{Q/V}$: doubling participation multiplies impact by $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$. It is an empirical rule of thumb, not physics — but the right order of magnitude for sizing execution costs.

questions.prompt: An order rests at the best bid. A large market sell sweeps the entire bid level and trades through to lower prices. Your resting order was:
options: filled at your limit price before any order behind you
filled at the lower sweep price
questions.explanation: Time priority: you were ahead in the queue, so you were filled fully at *your* price. The sweep's lower prices applied to the orders behind you — this is exactly why queue position has value.

questions.prompt: A backtest assumes maker fills whenever price trades through your level. With 2,000 lots ahead of you at that price and 1,200 lots traded there, did you fill? (1 = yes, 0 = no.)
questions.explanation: No: volume (1,200) never exceeded the queue ahead of you (2,000). Honest queue simulation requires traded volume to consume your position — the naive assumption is the single most common maker-backtest illusion.

questions.prompt: Displayed depth in the book is best understood as:
options: a firm commitment you can always trade through
a standing offer to maybe trade, withdrawable at any time
questions.explanation: Limit orders are free to cancel. The visible book overstates the liquidity you can actually transact — which is why impact models, execution algos and 'depth you can trade' all discount the display.
